4.51.m:
Skanda said:
Hear another [story], O fortunate one: the origin of Yamāditya,
by even hearing which a man never sees the world of Yama.
To the west of Yameśa and to the east of Vīreśa, O sage,
a man who beholds Yamāditya does not see the world of Yama.
A man who bathes in Yamatīrtha on the fourteenth day [of a fortnight] on a Tuesday,
and beholds Yameśvara, is quickly freed from all sins.
Formerly, having performed exceedingly pure austerity at Yamatīrtha,
Yama installed Yameśa and Yamāditya, who grant success to devotees.
Since the sun was established there by Yama, O pot-born one [Agastya],
for that reason, indeed, Yamāditya removes the torment inflicted by Yama.
Bowing to Yameśa and Yamāditya established by Yama,
and having bathed at Yamatīrtha, he does not see the world of Yama.
At Yamatīrtha, on the fourteenth day [of a fortnight] in the asterism of Bharaṇī on a Tuesday,
having offered libations and balls of rice, one becomes free of debt to the ancestors.
Ancestors dwelling in hell constantly yearn:

4.51.m:
‘If on a Tuesday, under Bharaṇī, on the fourteenth day [of the fortnight], this supreme conjunction occurs,
may some wise person, having bathed at Yamatīrtha in Kāśī,
offer a water libation with sesame seeds for our liberation!’
What need have men of journeys to Gayā? What need of ancestral rites with lavish priestly gifts,
if an ancestral rite is obtained at Yamatīrtha in Kāśī during this conjunction?
Having performed an ancestral rite at Yamatīrtha, having worshipped Yameśvara,
and having bowed to Yamāditya, one becomes free of debt to the ancestors.
Skanda said:
Thus the twelve Ādityas, destroyers of sin, have been described to you,
by hearing whose origins a man will never fall into hell.
There are others also, O jar-born one, established in Kāśī
in large numbers by devotees of the sun, such as Guhyakārka and the rest.
Having heard these meritorious chapters indicating the twelve Ādityas,
or having recited them to others, a mortal never goes to an evil destiny anywhere.

Now begins the second half of the glorious Kāśīkhaṇḍa.
Homage to the glorious Gaṇeśa.
Agasti said:
O delight of Pārvatī's heart! O lord born of the body of the Omniscient One!
I desire to ask something, O Master; you ought to tell it. 1
She was the daughter of Dakṣa Prajāpati and the wife of Kaśyapa,
the virtuous mother of Garutmat: how did she fall into servitude? 2
Skanda said:
How the ascetic Vinatā was reduced to the status of a menial maidservant,
that too I shall relate, O wise one; listen! 3
Long ago, Kadrū bore a hundred sons from Kaśyapa;
Vinatā gave birth to three: Ulūka, Aruṇa, and Tārkṣya. 4
Although the owl obtained kingship, O sage, because he was the chief among birds,
he was deposed from the kingship by all of them because he lacked virtues: 5
"This one has cruel eyes, this one is blind by day, and he always has crooked talons;
the speech of this one causes extreme distress to everyone." 6
Having thus censured his collection of qualities in many ways, the free-flying birds
even today do not choose anyone for their king. 7
When that happened to the owl, eager to see her child,
Vinatā then broke open the middle egg. 8
Breaking it when a thousand years were completed [was proper], O pot-born one,
[yet] out of impatience she broke that egg in the eighth century [of years]. 9
By that time, all the limbs of that exceedingly radiant infant
above the thighs had been formed, while dwelling within the shell. 10
The moment he came out of the egg, with the radiant beauty of his face red with fury,
the infant, whose body was half-formed, cursed his mother: 11
"O mother, because seeing the sons of Kadrū playing in their own sport
upon their mother's lap, you split the egg in two, 12
therefore, since all my limbs are unformed, I curse you, O bird:
become the slave woman of those very sons born of your co-wife's body here!" 13
Then, trembling from that curse, the bird said this:
"O thighless one! Tell me, mother's child, the end of the curse!" 14

Anūru said:
“Do not break the third egg, for I am indeed still unformed!
He who will be [born] in this egg shall remove your servitude.”
Having said this, that Aruṇa flew away and went to the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana),
where the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara) would grant a fortunate destiny even to a lame person.
This cause of Vinatā's servitude has been related to you who asked.
Sage, in connection [with this] I shall tell the origin of Aruṇāditya.
Since he lacked thighs, he is Anūru; because he was red with rage, he is Aruṇa.
Having performed austerity in Vārāṇasī, he worshipped the Maker of the Day (the Sun).
He too, being pleased, then granted boons to that Anūru,
and the sun, after his name, came to be known as Aruṇāditya.
Arka (the Sun) said:
“Stay on my chariot forever, O Anūru, son of Vinatā,
for the welfare of the worlds, destroying the darkness ahead.
Those men who will worship your image installed here
in Vārāṇasī, to the north of Mahādeva—whence could they have any fear?
Those who will constantly worship me here named Aruṇāditya
shall have no sorrow, no poverty, and no sin.
They are not overcome by diseases, nor by any afflictions;
they are not burned by the fire of grief, indeed, through serving Aruṇāditya.”
Then, placing Aruṇa on his chariot, Ravi took him away.
Even today he rises early in the morning on the chariot of the Sun.
Whoever rises early in the morning and bows day after day
to Aruṇa accompanied by Sūrya—whence could he have sorrow or fear?
The best of men who listens to this Aruṇāditya-māhātmya
shall never incur any wrongdoing whatsoever.
Skanda said:
Listen, I shall tell you the māhātmya of Vṛddhāditya,
by merely hearing which a man will not incur wrongdoing.
Long ago here in Vārāṇasī, Vṛddhahārīta, a man of great austerity,
worshipped Ravi for the enhancement of his great austerity.

Having installed an auspicious image of the Sun that possesses auspicious marks
to the south of Viśālākṣī, endowed with firm devotion,
Bradhna (the Sun), pleased, offered a boon to that old ascetic:
“Without delay, ask: what boon should I give to you?”
Then that sage chose a boon from the pleased jewel of the sky:
“If the Blessed One is pleased, give me youth again!
Because as an old man I do not have the capacity to perform austerity;
having attained youth once more, I shall perform supreme austerity.
Austerity alone is the highest dharma; austerity alone is the highest wealth;
austerity alone is the highest desire; austerity alone is indeed nirvāṇa.
Without austerity, are riches and good fortune obtainable anywhere?
The station of Dhruva and others was attained solely through the power of austerity.
Therefore I will perform austerity which grants greatness in both worlds,
having obtained youth, approved by all, through the granting of your boon.
Fie upon old age for living beings here, by which everyone becomes detached!
When the group of senses is afflicted by old age, even women do not submit to one's control.
Better indeed were death; let there not be old age, which causes extreme misery!
Death is pain for a moment, but old age is pain at every single moment.
Those who have conquered their senses desire a long life for prolonged austerity,
wealth for charity, a wife for a son, [and] intellect for liberation.”
Instantly taking away that old age of the old man, Bradhna
gave him youth, the cause of charm and the means to merit.
Thus that great sage Vṛddhahārīta in Vārāṇasī,
having obtained youth from Bradhna, performed fierce austerity.
Because the Sun, the remover of old age,
was worshipped by the aged ascetic Hārīta, he is therefore remembered as Vṛddhāditya.
Having worshipped Vṛddhāditya in Vārāṇasī, O Pot-born [Agastya],
which destroys old age, misfortune, and disease, many have attained perfection.

Skanda said:
Listen next, O sage, to the supreme Keśavāditya,
and how Savitṛ, having reached Keśava, attained knowledge.
Once, as he traversed the sky, the seven-horsed [Sun] saw
Ādikeśava worshipping the liṅga of Īśvara.
As if out of curiosity, descending from the sky, Ravi approached,
silent, motionless, composed, filled with great astonishment.
Awaiting an opportunity, wishing to ask Hari something,
when Hari had concluded his worship, he bowed with folded hands.
Hari said “Welcome to you” with great respect,
and made the Sun, who had his neck bowed, sit near himself.
Then, perceiving an occasion, the Eye of the World (the Sun),
having bowed to Adhokṣaja and received permission from the enemy of the Asuras, made this petition:
Ravi said:
“You are the inner self of the worlds, O All-Sustainer, Lord of the Universe!
Do you too have someone worthy of worship, O Mādhava, who are worshipped by the universe?
From you this all manifests, and in you everything dissolves;
you alone are the protector of the entire world, O treasure-house of the worlds!
Seeing this wonder, I have come here to your presence.
What is this being worshipped by you, O Lord, you who remove the affliction of worldly existence?”
Having heard this spoken by the thousand-rayed [Sun], Hṛṣīkeśa,
checking the seven-horsed [Sun] with a hand gesture, spoke aloud:
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
“The God of gods, Mahādeva, the blue-throated Lord of Umā,
he alone is indeed to be worshipped here, the cause of all causes.
Here, the fool who worships someone other than the Three-Eyed One
is to be known as truly bereft of eyes, even though he has eyes.
Mṛtyuñjaya alone is to be worshipped, the remover of birth, death, and old age;
indeed, having worshipped Mṛtyuñjaya, Śveta became victorious over death.
Having worshipped the Death of Death, Bhṛṅgin truly conquered death;
Death also abandoned Śailādi, the worshipper of Mṛtyuñjaya.”

/ Sons, wives, fields, heaven, and even liberation, without a doubt! / The abundance of the sovereignty of the three worlds was attained by me, O thousand-rayed one, / solely through the worship of the liṅga of Śiva—this is truth, truth, again and again! / This alone is the highest yoga, this alone is the supreme austerity, / this alone is the highest knowledge: that the liṅga of Sthāṇu is worshipped. / By whomsoever the liṅga of Pārvatī's lord has been worshipped even once here, / whence could there be any fear of suffering for them in this transmigration, which is a vessel of sorrow? In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, upon the first lunar day,
having bathed at Daśāśvamedhika, one is freed from the sins of a lifetime.
In Jyeṣṭha, on the second day of the bright fortnight, having bathed in Rudrasaras,
the sin committed in two lifetimes is destroyed that very moment.
Bathing thus sequentially on all the lunar days, the best of men,
up to the tenth day of the bright fortnight, would cast off the sin of lifetime after lifetime.
Reaching the lunar day Daśaharā, which takes away the sins of ten lifetimes,
one who has bathed at Daśāśvamedhika will not see torment inflicted by Yama.
Having seen the liṅga Daśāśvamedheśa on the Daśaharā lunar day,
one is abandoned by sins accumulated over ten lifetimes; of this there is no doubt.
He who, having bathed on Daśaharā, would worship the supreme liṅga,
Daśāśvamedheśa, with devotion—the condition of the womb shall not touch him.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, in the bright fortnight, a man at Rudrasaras
performing the annual pilgrimage for a fortnight is not overcome by obstacles.

4.52.m:
Whatever fruit is properly obtained through the final ablutions of ten horse-sacrifices,
that indeed is obtained having bathed at Daśāśvamedha on the Daśaharā lunar day.
On the western bank of the celestial river, having bowed to Daśahareśvara,
a most meritorious man never meets with an evil plight.
At that which is celebrated as the southern gate of the inner sanctuary in Kāśī,
having seen Brahmeśvara there, one is magnified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus, in the guise of a brahmin in Vārāṇasī, the great-minded
Druhiṇa remained until the arrival of the Lord of the Universe.
Divodāsa also, a king of kings, for the brahmin who had performed the sacrifices,
for Brahmā in the form of an old brahmin, constructed an abode for Brahmā.
Near Brahmeśvara was a delightful hall of Brahmā;
Brahmā dwelt there, filling the sky with resonances of Vedic chanting.
Thus to you has been spoken, O brahmin, the exceedingly great majesty
of the Daśāśvamedha sacred ford, which destroys the masses of all sins.

What calculation then can be made of any other god? / With a glance I burned Kāma, the conqueror of the three worlds; / alas, longing for Kāśī torments me even more! / Whom indeed can I dispatch from here to investigate news of Kāśī? / Who indeed is skilled to discern it, except the four-faced one [Brahmā]?’ / Thus summoning the Creator with great respect / and seating him there, Śrīkaṇṭha spoke to the four-faced one: / ‘The yoginīs were sent previously; then the thousand-rayed sun was sent; / even today they do not return from Kāśī, O pot-born one! / That Kāśī stirs longing in my mind, O lord of the world, / like some fickle-eyed maiden stirs an ordinary man! / Here on Mandara, in this lovely cave, I find no great delight, / like a crocodile in a shallow pond of impure, turbid water! / The heat born of the hālāhala poison did not afflict me so, / as the anguish born of separation from Kāśī intensely afflicts me here! / Even though seated on my head, raining drops of nectar, / the cool-rayed moon is unable, alas, to dispel the heat born of separation from Kāśī! / O Creator, execute my task, O noble, foremost, wise one! / Go quickly from here to Kāśī, and strive for my desire! / O Brahmā, you alone know the reason for leaving Kāśī; / even a fool would not leave Kāśī, let alone one who understands anything! / Why should I not go to Kāśī this very day by my own māyā, O Brahmā? / But I do not wish to transgress King Divodāsa, who abides by his duty! / O Creator, since you yourself arrange all things that must be arranged, / saying “do this” and “do that” to you is altogether pointless!’

4.52.m:
"Go without obstacle; let your path have an auspicious outcome!"
Taking the command upon his head, Brahmā went to Vārāṇasī with joy.
Quickly reaching the city of Vārāṇasī with his white-swan chariot,
the self-born Brahmā then considered himself to have achieved his purpose.
"Today the fruit of having a swan as my mount has been realized upon reaching Kāśī;
for at every step, obstacles are said to arise on the path to Kāśī.
Today the root *dṛś* ['to see'] has become meaningful in connection with my eyes,
since this pleasure-garden has clearly entered my field of vision—
which the river of heaven itself sprinkles with its waters,
where the trees are made of bliss, where the people are made of bliss!
In Kāśī they constantly enjoy blissful fruits as well;
Kāśī is forever the ground of bliss, and Śiva is forever the giver of bliss.
Therefore, living beings born in Kāśī are indeed embodiments of bliss.
Those alone are feet known to walk among the fortunate here,
which would walk about the earthly city of the Sustainer of the Universe.
Those alone are ears known as greatly learned in knowledge,
by which Kāśī has been heard of once in this world among men versed in the Vedas.
That alone thinks of everything, which is the mind among the wise in this world,
by which this Kāśī, the ground of all authorities, is acknowledged.
That intelligence alone understands everything here among the wise and virtuous,
by which this abode of Dhūrjaṭi is held and made its object.
Far better are those blades of grass and grains, even if tossed by a whirlwind,
that fall here in Kāśī, than men who have never seen Kāśī!
Today my lifespan, measured at two parārdhas, has borne fruit,
since during its course the city of Kāśikā, so difficult to reach, was reached by me!
Ah, the wealth of my merit! Ah, the greatness of my good fortune,
that today I have seen Kāśī, so long contemplated!
Today the tree of my austerity has borne abundant, truly great fruits
consisting of the fruits of my desires, sprinkled with the water of devotion to Śiva.

4.52.m:
"Many kinds of creation were made by me as I unfolded the universe;
but Kāśī is unique, fashioned by the Lord of the Universe Himself."
With his mind delighted thus after seeing the city of Vārāṇasī,
the Creator, in the form of an old brahmin, saw the king.
With his hand holding water and unhusked barley-grains, having spoken a blessing to the ruler of the earth,
he was saluted with reverence by the king, and then sat on the seat offered by him.
Honored by the king with rising to greet him, offering a seat, and so forth,
the brahmin addressed the king, who asked the reason for his arrival:

The brahmin said:
"O protector of the earth, I have been here for a very long time; I am an ancient resident.
You, however, do not know me at all, but I know you, Ripuñjaya!
More than a hundred kings have been seen by me, who gave lavish priestly gifts,
conquered numerous battles, performed sacrifices, and controlled their senses;
who had cast out the group of six inner enemies, were of noble conduct, rich in virtue,
had crossed to the far shore of Vedic learning, and were skilled in statecraft;
who were adept in compassion and courtesy, dedicated to the vow of truth,
equal to the earth in forgiveness, and surpassed the ocean in profundity;
who conquered the surge of anger, were heroic, and were abodes of gentle beauty;
endowed with such virtues, who had well amassed the wealth of renown.
Yet, O royal sage, those two or three holy virtues of yours—
they have mostly not come into my sight among any of those kings!
Your subjects are your own family; you revere brahmins as deities;
you are an ally of great austerity: other kings were not of this path.
You are blessed and respected by the good; you are worthy of worship for your noble virtues.
Even the gods, O Divodāsa, do not wander from the path out of fear of you!
What need have we, desireless brahmins, of praising you, O king?
What can we do? The multitude of your virtues turns us into panegyrists!
Let this discourse rest for now; I shall speak of the matter at hand.
I wish to perform a sacrifice, O king, and therefore I choose you as my helper.
With you as its ruler, this earth is an abode of all prosperity.

4.52.m:
"And I possess abundant wealth, O king, great wealth acquired righteously.
And this capital of yours is supreme in the land of ritual action;
in it, whatever deeds are performed do not perish even at the dissolution of the world.
Whatever wealth is accumulated by men walking the noble path of righteousness
should be applied in Kāśī; otherwise it will lead only to distress.
No one knows the supreme greatness of Kāśī, O lord of the earth,
except the three-eyed Śambhu, who bestows all knowledge.
I consider you most blessed, since by meritorious deeds earned across hundreds of births
you protect Kāśī, the supreme body of the Sustainer of the Universe.
Kāśī is the essence of the three worlds, the very essence of the three Vedas,
and the supreme essence beyond the three goals of life—so it has been determined by the great seers.
Only by the grace of the Lord of the Universe is this city protected by you.
From the protection of even one person in Kāśī, the three worlds become protected.
Furthermore, I tell you what is beneficial, if it pleases you, O blameless one:
the Lord of the Universe alone should always be pleased by all actions.
Never look upon the Lord of the Universe as another deity, O king!
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, the moon, and the sun are merely the play of that Dhūrjaṭi.
Because kings are to be instructed by brahmins who desire good future outcomes,
therefore what is beneficial to you has been spoken. Or what is this concern to me?"
To the brahmin who thus remained silent, the best of kings replied:
"Everything that was spoken by you, O best of brahmins, has been held in my heart."
The king said:
"To you who desire to sacrifice, in the matter of your assistance,
I am a servant; not one among a hundred sacrificial materials is missing.
Whatever is mine, in all the seven constituents of the realm, you are the master over it.
Perform your sacrifice with a single mind, O brahmin; consider your wish accomplished!
That I rule the kingdom, O brahmin, is not in the least for my own sake;
with my sons, my wives, and my body, I strive for the benefit of others.
For kings, even above sacrificial rites and even above all sacred fords everywhere,
the protection of the subjects alone has been proclaimed by the wise as the one duty."

4.52.m: "The fire born of distress among subjects is more terrible even than the fire of a thunderbolt; / the fire of a thunderbolt burns two or three, but the former consumes a kingdom, family, and body. / When I am about to take the avabhṛtha bath, O best of brahmins, / I then perform an ablution with the water from the feet of brahmins. / The oblation I make into the mouth of a brahmin, O best among the twice-born— / I consider that superior even to sacrificial rites, O great-minded one. / Among all desires, one keeps vigil here in my heart: / even today, some petitioner asking even for my own body must be seen. / Oh, after many days my wish has borne fruit, / since today you have arrived at my house to make a request, O brahmin. / With a focused mind, O brahmin, perform many sacrifices / with lavish sacrificial fees; know that assistance is given in all matters." / Having heard this speech of the deeply wise, righteous king, / the Creator, pleased in mind, brought together the provisions for the sacrifice. / Having received the assistance of the royal seer Divodāsa, the lotus-born [Brahmā] / sacrificed in Kāśī with ten horse-sacrifices, great sacrificial rites. / The space of the sky was filled with masses of sacrificial smoke even then; / from that time on, this sky has not lost its blueness. / The sacred ford named Daśāśvamedha became renowned across the earthly realm; / from that time on it existed in Vārāṇasī, bestowing auspiciousness. / Formerly, O pot-born [Agastya], that sacred ford was known as Rudrasaras; 4.52.m: and having established Brahmeśvara, the Creator remained right there. / "Kāśī is determined to be the supreme body of the Lord of the Universe; / from serving it, Śambhu will not be angry with me in person. / What foolish person, having attained Kāśī, would ever wish to abandon it here again, / capable [as it is] of uprooting karma generated through many births? / In the abode of the Lord of the Universe, who destroys the distress of the universe, his body / is sorely tormented by the great fire born of separation from Kāśī. / But whoever, having attained Kāśī, which destroys the mass of all sins, would abandon it, / should be recognized as a beast in human form, turning his back on supreme joy. / Whoever desires the fortune of nirvāṇa, leaving behind the misery of saṃsāra, / must not abandon Kāśī if it is obtained by the grace of Īśa. / That fool who, completely abandoning Kāśī, would go elsewhere— / from the palm of his hand departs the rising fruit of the four aims of life. / Destroyer of a multitude of sins, enhancer of immense merit, / bestower of the bliss of liberation—having reached Kāśī, what foolish person would abandon it? / Where is such bliss in Satyaloka? Where is bliss in the abode of Viṣṇu, / as that bliss which is obtained in Kāśī by worshipping for half a moment?" / Having thus resolved upon the multitude of virtues of Vārāṇasī, Druhiṇa [Brahmā], / turning away, did not return again to Mount Mandara, O sage. / Skanda said: / O son of Mitra and Varuṇa, I shall tell you the greatness / of Daśāśvamedha in Kāśī, the crest-jewel of all sacred fords. / Having reached Daśāśvamedhika, the best of the best of all sacred fords, / whatever action is performed is said to be imperishable here. / Bathing, giving gifts, silent recitation, oblations into the fire, study of the Vedas, worship of deities, / twilight prayers, water libations, ancestral rites, and honoring the ancestors— / having bathed once at the sacred ford of Daśāśvamedhika, the best among men,

4.56.m: As you slept at night in the fourth watch, a great lake

And oh, the shaven-headed person in reddish-brown robes who was seen by you,

A solar eclipse was seen at night, which surely brings great calamity;

The sun, having arrived in the west, struck down to the earth's surface
the cool-rayed moon rising in the sky; that indicates danger to the kingdom.
The pair of comets that was seen fighting each other
simultaneously is not auspicious; it leads solely to the ruin of the realm.
That you saw yourself with your hair and teeth falling out,
and being led toward the south, is terrifying even for your family.
The breaking of the palace banner that was seen by you at night's end,
know that to cause the ruin of the kingdom, destined for a great disaster.
In a dream the city was flooded by the waves of the ocean of milk;

Since in a dream you were carried southward by a vehicle drawn by monkeys,
therefore, O wise one, abandoning the city is the means to avert it.
